## Guidelines

### Code

Code should follow the [tidyverse style](https://style.tidyverse.org/).
Particularly,

-   there should be spaces before and line breaks after each `+` when building a `ggplot`,
-   there should also be spaces before and line breaks after each `|>` in a data transformation pipeline,
-   code should be properly indented,
-   there should be spaces around `=` signs and spaces after commas.

Additionally, all code should be visible in the PDF output, i.e., should not run off the page on the PDF.
Long lines that run off the page should be split across multiple lines with line breaks.[^1]

[^1]: Remember, haikus not novellas when writing code!

### Plots

-   Plots should have an informative title and, if needed, also a subtitle.
-   Axes and legends should be labeled with both the variable name and its units (if applicable).
-   Careful consideration should be given to aesthetic choices.

### Workflow

Continuing to develop a sound workflow for reproducible data analysis is important as you complete the lab and other assignments in this course.

-   You should have at least 3 commits with meaningful commit messages by the end of the assignment.
-   Final versions of both your `.qmd` file and the rendered PDF should be pushed to GitHub.

# Questions

## Question 1

For this question, you will work with the following dataset called `scores`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
scores <- tribble(
  ~student_id , ~math , ~english ,
  "S1"        ,    90 ,       92 ,
  "S2"        ,    85 ,       80 ,
  "S3"        ,    88 ,       85 ,
  "S4"        ,    95 ,       74
)

scores
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  student_id  math english
  <chr>      <dbl>   <dbl>
1 S1            90      92
2 S2            85      80
3 S3            88      85
4 S4            95      74
```


:::
:::


::: callout-note
The `tribble()` function is helpful for creating small data frames (`tibble`s) with an easier to read row-by-row layout.
:::

It has three variables (`student_id`, `math`, and `english`) and four rows (one for each student).

Before writing any code, answer the following questions:

- Suppose you want to reshape the data frame so that there is one row per student per subject.
  What function would you use to do this?

- If you reshaped the data to have one row per student per subject, 
  - how many rows would the resulting data frame have?
  - how many columns would the resulting data frame have and what would the column names be?

Then, write the code to reshape the data frame as described above.

## Question 2

For this question, you will work with the following dataset called `patients`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
patients <- tribble(
  ~patient_id , ~measurement_time_ , ~systolic_bp ,
  "P1"        , "Morning"          ,          120 ,
  "P1"        , "Noon"             ,          115 ,
  "P1"        , "Evening"          ,          123 ,
  "P2"        , "Morning"          ,          118 ,
  "P2"        , "Evening"          ,          121
)

patients
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 × 3
  patient_id measurement_time_ systolic_bp
  <chr>      <chr>                   <dbl>
1 P1         Morning                   120
2 P1         Noon                      115
3 P1         Evening                   123
4 P2         Morning                   118
5 P2         Evening                   121
```


:::
:::


It has three variables (`patient_id`, `measurement_time_`, and `systolic_bp` -- short for systolic blood pressure) and five rows (one per patient per measurement time).

Before writing any code, answer the following questions:

- Suppose you want to reshape the data frame so that there is one row per patient and measurements at different times of the day are recorded in different columns.
  What function would you use to do this?

- If you reshaped the data to have one row per patient, 
  - how many rows would the resulting data frame have?
  - how many columns would the resulting data frame have and what would the column names be?

Then, write the code to reshape the data frame as described above. What does the `NA` value mean in the resulting data frame?

## Question 3

For this question, you will work with the following dataset called `quiz_scores`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
quiz_scores <- tribble(
  ~student_id , ~week_1 , ~week_2 , ~week_3 ,
  "S1"        , "80"    , "85"    , "90"    ,
  "S2"        , "75"    , NA      , "88"    ,
  "S3"        , "92"    , "90"    , "95"
)

quiz_scores
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  student_id week_1 week_2 week_3
  <chr>      <chr>  <chr>  <chr> 
1 S1         80     85     90    
2 S2         75     <NA>   88    
3 S3         92     90     95    
```


:::
:::


It has one row per student and one column for each week's quiz score.
Notice that the scores are stored as character strings (in quotation marks), and one score is missing.

You want to reshape this data frame to have one row per student per week and three columns: `student_id`, `week`, and `score`.
The `week` column should contain the integers `1`, `2`, and `3`, and `score` should be numeric.
Keep the row corresponding to the missing score.

a. Before writing any code, answer the following questions:

  - What function would you use to reshape the data, and how many rows would the resulting data frame have?
  - If you only specified which columns to pivot and the new column names, what values and data type would you expect in `week`? What data type would you expect in `score`?

Then, complete the following steps:

b. Read about `names_prefix`, `names_transform`, and `values_transform` in the documentation for `pivot_longer()`. Reshape `quiz_scores` as described above using these arguments within a single `pivot_longer()` call, and save the result as `quiz_scores_long`.

::: callout-tip
Hint: `as.integer()` converts values to integers, and `as.numeric()` converts values to numbers. Supply transformation functions without parentheses, using the form `list(column_name = function_name)`.
:::

c. Display `quiz_scores_long` and use `glimpse()` to check the column types.Explain what each of the three new arguments does and why removing the prefix alone is not enough to make `week` an integer.

d. Reshape `quiz_scores_long` back to one row per student, with columns named `week_1`, `week_2`, and `week_3`. Use `names_prefix` in `pivot_wider()` to restore the prefix. How does the role of `names_prefix` differ between the two pivot functions? How do the score column types in this result compare with those in the original `quiz_scores`?
